paras: The threatened lynching of Ernest Chappell took place at Fitzpatrick, in Twiggs County, Georgia, around August 1, 1915, when a mob formed to take Chappell, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and lynch him. Sheriff Wimberly moved Chappell and the jail's only other inmate, Will Thomas, to the Bibb County jail in Macon before the mob acted. The episode reached the press as a short Macon dispatch printed in Georgia and South Carolina.

Chappell was held in the Twiggs County jail at Fitzpatrick on a charge of attempting to criminally assault the wife of a farmer the Americus Times-Recorder called "prominent." The version printed in Sumter, South Carolina, described the woman as white and said Chappell "is said to have confessed" to the attempt, without naming who made that claim. Thomas, also Black, was jailed on a charge of stealing a cow.

According to the Macon dispatch, the sheriff learned that a mob was organizing at Fitzpatrick to lynch Chappell. The two prisoners were then "rushed" to Macon at midnight for safekeeping, a trip the Americus paper placed "this morning." Thomas was taken along because officials thought the mob "might taken vengeance on him when they found Chappell gone."
No violence at Fitzpatrick is reported, and no arrests of mob members, trial of Chappell or later disposition of either prisoner appears in the coverage.

The Americus Times-Recorder ran the story on its front page on August 2 under the headline "Negroes Wanted by Mob Rushed to Macon Jail." Two days later the Sumter Watchman and Southron printed a Macon dispatch dated August 1 as "Negroes in Danger," with a deck calling Chappell an "Alleged Assailant" and Thomas "One Who Stole Cow." Both papers repeated the charges against the prisoners, and neither commented on the mob.
No Black-press report of the episode was found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Ernest Chappell
bases: A mob was reported organizing to take Chappell from the Twiggs county jail and lynch him, and the sheriff removed him to Macon before it acted (A1, A2).

A mob formed to lynch Chappell over an accusation of attempted assault on a white woman, but he was moved to the Bibb county jail and no one was killed (A1, A2); this is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.
Two papers, Americus and Sumter, carry Macon dispatches that agree on the prisoners, the charges, the mob and the removal to Macon, though both likely derive from the same Macon wire source (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Macon wire report
accounts.gist: A mob was forming at Fitzpatrick to take Chappell from jail and lynch him; the sheriff took him and Will Thomas to Macon for safekeeping.

framing.detail: The Americus Times-Recorder ran the Macon dispatch on page one as 'Negroes Wanted by Mob Rushed to Macon Jail', presenting the removal without comment on the mob.
The Sumter Watchman and Southron headed it 'Negroes in Danger' with the deck 'Threatened Lynching Directed at Alleged Assailant and One Who Stole Cow', stating Thomas's theft as fact in the deck.

versions.value: Brought to Macon 'this morning' (paper of Aug. 2; dispatch date cut off)
Rushed to Macon 'at midnight', dispatch dated Macon, Aug. 1

conflicts.note: Probably the same night transfer; the Aug. 1 dateline places it in the night of July 31-Aug. 1 or early Aug. 1, not Aug. 2.

'Said to have confessed' that he attempted to assault a white woman

conflicts.note: Not contradictory; the reported confession appears only in the Sumter version and is unattributed.

record_check.dossier: The Macon dispatch is dated Aug. 1 and says the prisoners were moved at midnight; Aug. 1 (or the night before) is better supported than Aug. 2, which is the Americus print date.
Full name Will Thomas, charged with cow stealing.
